youtube.title: His Defense: The Vermeer Was His Own Forgery
youtube.titleSupport: Required YouTube title; Facebook title only if a separate live field exists
youtube.description:
His defense was that the supposed masterpiece was his own forgery.

In 1945, Han van Meegeren was arrested on suspicion of collaboration after a supposed Vermeer reached Hermann Göring through an art dealer. Technical evidence supported his confession: old supports did not make modern resin-based paint centuries old. The collaboration case fell away; in 1947 he was convicted of fraud and forgery and sentenced to one year.

The Supper at Emmaus shown here illustrates earlier expert acceptance. It is not the painting sold to Göring. No courtroom painting demonstration or execution deadline is claimed.

Sources:
Metropolitan Museum of Art, Art Forgery (1968): https://resources.metmuseum.org/resources/metpublications/pdf/Art_Forgery_The_Metropolitan_Museum_of_Art_Bulletin_v_26_no_6_February_1968.pdf
Contemporary trial reporting, TIME (1947): https://time.com/archive/6823954/art-truth-consequences/
Froentjes & de Wild, Chemisch Weekblad 45 (1949), pp.269–277: report by court-appointed examiners.

Archival photographs: Bram Wisman and Koos Raucamp / Anefo, Nationaal Archief (CC0).
AI-generated narration; authentic archival photographs and original explanatory graphics. Diagrams are schematic, not historical laboratory footage.

instagram.description:
To defend himself, he had to prove the supposed masterpiece was a fake.

Han van Meegeren’s confession challenged paintings experts had accepted as Vermeers. Investigators found evidence of modern synthetic resin and separate crack networks in old and newer paint layers. An old canvas did not make the painting an old master.

The collaboration case fell away. The fraud did not: he was convicted of fraud and forgery in 1947 and sentenced to one year.

The Supper at Emmaus is shown to explain earlier expert acceptance; it is not the painting sold to Göring.

Sources: Froentjes & de Wild (1949), court examiners’ report; Metropolitan Museum of Art, Art Forgery (1968); TIME, Truth & Consequences (1947).

facebook.description:
A supposed Vermeer reached Hermann Göring through an art dealer. Han van Meegeren’s defense: he had painted it himself.

Investigators examined materials and crack patterns. Old supports concealed modern resin-based paint. The evidence supported his confession, but did not make him innocent: in 1947 he was convicted of fraud and forgery and sentenced to one year.

Emmaus, shown here as an example of earlier expert acceptance, was not the painting sold to Göring.

Sources: Froentjes & de Wild, court examiners’ report (1949); Metropolitan Museum of Art, Art Forgery (1968); contemporary TIME trial report: https://time.com/archive/6823954/art-truth-consequences/

Archival photographs: Bram Wisman and Koos Raucamp / Anefo, Nationaal Archief (CC0).
